title: Microsoft-backed AI data center faces backlash over 62 unpermitted gas turbines
content:
Microsoft-backed AI data center faces backlash over alleged unpermitted gas turbines and 1.5M-gallon LNG tank — groups' issues with $19.4B facility range from illegal construction to noise pollution
Microsoft is not being a good neighbor.
The DataOne data center in Vineland, New Jersey, has faced a slew of complaints from the community since construction began in 2025. According to Stand.earth, the project has reportedly been operating several unpermitted gas turbines on site, spewing air pollution in the area near two local schools. Aside from that, the site has also faced allegations of constructing an unpermitted 1.5-million-gallon liquefied natural gas storage tank and of unacceptable noise levels at night, which affected residents within a half-mile radius of the data center.
Matt Williams, chairperson of the Sustain South Jersey group, told Tom’s Hardware that construction had already begun even before Nebius signed a multi-year agreement to “deliver dedicated capacity to Microsoft from its new data center in Vineland, New Jersey,” in October 2025. However, the residents only became aware that the project was a data center after the $19.4 billion deal to secure around 100,000 Nvidia GB300 GPUs for the tech giant was made public.
Vineland residents began seeing references to the data center in various government documents, prompting several questions to the city government. Because of this, the city called a town hall meeting last January 2026 — several months after construction on the data center had already begun, with DataOne CEO Charles-Antoine Beyney admitting that the meeting should have been initiated several months before.
A few weeks before the town hall, some people living within a half-mile radius of the site started complaining about noise from the development. While they couldn’t confirm the source of the noise, it was often described as a low hum, similar to that of a generator. A later investigation revealed that the site had 62 gas turbines deployed in the area, with at least 45 running at any given time. This is similar to what SpaceXAI has done in Memphis, Tennessee, where it deployed 69 unpermitted natural gas turbines to power its data centers. While the company has since promised to remove these polluting generators, it will do so only over a span of one year, as they’re being slowly replaced by a 1.2-GW on-site power plant.
There have also been concerns that the site’s stormwater management system does not comply with the state’s regulations. A third-party engineering review stated that if these issues are not fixed, they could result in on-site and off-site flooding, especially given the site’s massive 55-acre size. The experts also noted that the data center has “underestimated the annual groundwater recharge by at least 20 million gallons per year,” which could result in lower aquifer levels and reduce the amount of water available or the water quality for the people living in the area.
“The incident should shatter the illusion that Microsoft is a ‘good neighbor’ or in any way more responsible than the other Big Tech companies,” Stand.earth Senior Campaigner Nathan Taft said in the statement. “This investigation has revealed that far from ‘doing this work differently than other’ as it promised, Microsoft is drawing directly from Elon Musk’s xAI playbook of doing the damage first and asking for permission later.”
In an interview with Tom’s Hardware, Nathan said that even though Microsoft does not directly own or operate the Vineland data center, it stands to reason that the tech giant should do something about all these complaints, as it’s the one that has contracted Nebius for the computing power, which resulted in DataOne’s construction project. He compared this to a contractor making a mess on their client’s neighbor’s property. Even though a third-party provider — DataOne — was at fault for the issue, the fact that the people have already been complaining should give Nebius pause and compel Microsoft to do something.

DataOne’s actions in New Jersey directly contradict the promise Microsoft made back in January 2026, and residents are asking the tech giant to stand by its word. Although the concerns about air and noise pollution are technically not mentioned in the company’s “community-friendly” commitments, these issues still impact the quality of life of the people living around the DataOne data center. Aside from that, the unpermitted construction shows it does not adhere to the rules of Vineland. “The developers have been ‘act first, pay the fine, and ask for forgiveness later,’” says Mr. Williams.

Jowi Morales is a tech enthusiast with years of experience working in the industry. He’s been writing with several tech publications since 2021, where he’s been interested in tech hardware and consumer electronics.

report.summary: Microsoft-backed AI data center in Vineland, NJ faces backlash over unpermitted gas turbines, LNG tank, illegal construction, and noise pollution.
report.background: The DataOne data center in Vineland, New Jersey, is at the center of a community controversy. Construction began in 2025, but residents only learned it was a data center after Microsoft signed a $19.4 billion deal with Nebius for roughly 100,000 Nvidia GB300 GPUs. The project allegedly operates 62 unpermitted gas turbines, with at least 45 running at once, plus a 1.5-million-gallon LNG tank. Residents reported low-frequency noise within a half-mile radius, and a third-party review found stormwater management and groundwater recharge estimates may be understated. The pattern mirrors xAI's Memphis data center, which deployed 69 unpermitted turbines. Microsoft's earlier pledge to be "community-friendly" is being questioned, as the tech giant benefits from the computing capacity while developers allegedly act first and seek permission later.
key_points: Residents were kept in the dark during early construction. The data center was initially unidentified, and locals only learned about its true nature through government documents and the Microsoft-Nebius deal. A town hall was not held until months after work began, with DataOne's CEO admitting the meeting should have happened much earlier.

Unpermitted gas turbines are causing air and noise pollution. At least 45 of 62 deployed turbines regularly operate, creating a low hum disturbing people within a half-mile. The setup is similar to xAI's Memphis site, which prompted promises to replace generators with a cleaner power plant over a year.

Stormwater and groundwater concerns could affect flooding and water supply. The 55-acre site's stormwater system reportedly fails to meet state regulations, and the project underestimated annual groundwater recharge by at least 20 million gallons. Experts warn of on-site and off-site flooding and reduced aquifer levels.

Microsoft is under pressure despite not owning the facility. Stand.earth says Microsoft's "act first, ask forgiveness later" pattern contradicts its promises. Residents argue that because Microsoft contracted Nebius for AI capacity, it should ensure partners follow environmental and community rules.

The controversy highlights the hidden environmental costs of the AI boom. Large-scale GPU deployments demand enormous power and cooling, often using temporary fossil fuel generation to meet urgent timelines. This clashes with both community expectations and tech companies' stated sustainability goals.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this case shows that fast-scaling data center capacity can clash with local communities and environmental rules. Developers, including Microsoft's partners, may face stricter permitting scrutiny, legal challenges, and reputational damage. For developers, it underscores the need to consider sustainability and compliance when provisioning AI compute, as regional pushback can delay GPU deliveries or increase costs. For regular users, data center pollution and resource use affect air quality, noise, flooding risk, and groundwater in nearby neighborhoods. This incident also pressures major cloud providers to make their infrastructure investments more transparent and accountable, rather than outsourcing responsibility to third-party developers. It could lead to new regulations, community benefit agreements, or watchdog tools that make AI's footprint easier to track.
report.tools: For tracking AI data center environmental impact, watch Electricity Maps (open-source) to see grid carbon intensity by region. The Green Software Foundation's Carbon Aware SDK helps schedule compute workloads during cleaner energy periods. For estimating renewable potential at data center sites, NREL's PVWatts is a useful open calculator. Community groups can also use public permitting databases and AirNow for local pollution monitoring.
